item.title: Generative AI and Oral Proficiency: How ChatGPT Is Transforming English Language Speaking Practice
item.description: arXiv:2611.09898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into language learning contexts presents potential for developing oral proficiency, though empirical evidence regarding its efficacy remains limited. This quasi-experimental study investigated the impact of ChatGPT-mediated speaking practice on English oral proficiency among Iranian learners. A total of 380 participants (190 female, 190 male; M(age) = 21.4, SD = 4.7) from Tehran and Isfahan were assigned to experimental (ChatGPT practice; n = 190) or control (human pair work; n = 190) groups. Both groups completed an 8-week intervention with three 30-minute weekly sessions. Oral proficiency was assessed using a Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)-aligned Oral Proficiency Interview (OPI) scored on fluency, pronunciation, lexical resource, grammatical accuracy, and interactive communication (total score: 0-20). Multilevel growth modeling revealed a significant time-by-group interaction, F(1, 376) = 48.73, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .115. The experimental group demonstrated greater gains (M change = 2.90, SD = 1.60) than controls (M change = 0.75, SD = 1.80), d = 1.20, 95% CI [0.95, 1.45]. Gender moderated this effect, with females in the experimental group showing the largest improvements (M change = 2.50). Mediation analysis confirmed that increased integrative motivation partially mediated proficiency gains (indirect effect = 0.28, 95% CI [0.20, 0.36]). Findings indicate that structured ChatGPT practice yields modest but meaningful enhancements in oral proficiency, particularly when leveraging affective factors. Implications for AI-augmented speaking pedagogy in resource-constrained contexts are discussed.

item.title: Short-Form Video Exposure and Academic Strain: A Dose-Response Analysis and Acquiescence Diagnosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.09899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-form video platforms occupy a substantial share of undergraduate leisure time, raising concerns about sustained attention, deep learning, and academic well-being. However, much existing evidence relies on single-source Likert instruments with limited attention to response-style bias and measurement validity. This study analyses 863 university students who completed a 67-item, seven-construct battery assessing short-form content addiction, attention fragmentation, notification overload, cognitive fatigue, deep learning engagement, academic burnout, and self-regulation, alongside categorical exposure measures. A layered analytical protocol was implemented in Python, including descriptive screening, dimensionality assessment, reliability, convergent validity, careless-response diagnostics, and known-groups criterion validity. Daily exposure and in-study checking frequency showed consistent monotonic associations with maladaptive outcomes. Short-form content addiction exhibited the strongest effect ($\eta^2=0.117$, $\rho=0.273$, $p<0.001$), supported by nonparametric tests. However, the measurement analyses revealed substantial validity concerns: parallel analysis retained a single factor per construct, average variance extracted did not exceed 0.31, and a general agreement factor explained 59--89\% of construct variance. Controlling for this factor reversed the association between addiction and deep-learning engagement from $+0.55$ to $-0.49$. These findings indicate that short-form video exposure is associated with cognitive and academic strain, while response-style contamination can substantially distort theoretically meaningful relationships. The results highlight the need for balanced item wording, embedded response-quality controls, and explicit response-style modelling in behavioural-addiction research.
item.dc:creator: Md. Alamgir Hossain

item.title: KR A1: Design and Preliminary Evaluation of a Humanoid-Robot Interaction Prototype Integrating Personalized Voice Synthesis, Contextual Dialogue, and Emotion-Aware Response Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the design and preliminary evaluation of KR A1, a humanoid-robot interaction prototype that integrates personalized voice synthesis, contextual dialogue processing, and emotion-aware response generation for potential mental-healthcare applications. The system architecture combines a locally hosted large language model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, served via Ollama) for natural-language understanding and response generation, OpenVoice v2 for zero-shot speaker-adaptive speech synthesis, and a two-tier emotion-processing pipeline comprising a keyword heuristic and LLM-based inference. Face recognition (InsightFace) and vector memory retrieval (FAISS with sentence-transformer embeddings) enable user-personalized interaction. The experimental evaluation reported here is limited to the voice-cloning component: cloned voices were evaluated against reference recordings using eight acoustic similarity measures - mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, pitch, spectral centroid, spectral contrast, spectral rolloff, zero-crossing rate, formants, and speaker-embedding cosine similarity - supplemented by a same-speaker versus cross-speaker baseline comparison. All tests were conducted on a small, informal development sample; no statistical significance testing against a held-out baseline was performed. The emotion-recognition accuracy, end-to-end response latency, and therapeutic or clinical impact of the integrated system have not yet been formally evaluated and are identified as directions for future work. All testing was informal and self-conducted by the development team; no patients or external human participants were involved, and the system has not been evaluated or deployed in a clinical setting.
item.dc:creator: Mahek Aanthu, Om Aanthu, Aaryan AK Aanthu

item.title: CaregiverConnect: A Mobile Application for Stress Tracking and Support in Dementia Care
item.description: arXiv:2611.09901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rising global prevalence of dementia places escalating demands on paid professional caregivers, who frequently experience severe stress and professional isolation. Existing mobile health (mHealth) applications rarely integrate real-time stress monitoring with multimodal relief strategies. CaregiverConnect, a Flutter/Firebase mobile application comprising nine feature modules, was evaluated in a single-group, pre-post pilot study with 10 paid professional dementia caregivers at two nursing home facilities over two weeks. Descriptive analysis yielded an exploratory effect estimate for self-reported stress change (Cohen's d = 1.60; interpreted with caution given N = 10 and no control group), an improvement in emotional support responses from 60% to 100% of participants, and near-perfect usability ratings (UI Navigation: 4.90/5.0). These preliminary findings support the feasibility and acceptability of CaregiverConnect and identify end-of-shift stress peaks as a priority target for future adaptive design. Larger randomized controlled trials are needed to establish efficacy.
item.dc:creator: Yagna Manasa Boyapati, Arshia Khan

item.title: Human-AI Collaboration at Scale: Task Criticality, Agency, and Friction across 250,000 Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2611.09902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI is increasingly embedded in professional work, yet how people actually collaborate with it at scale remains poorly understood. Drawing on a corpus of 249,834 real-world conversations, we conduct privacy-preserving analysis by asking three questions: what work people bring to AI, what roles humans retain in completing that work, and where human-AI collaboration breaks down. We find that users bring to AI not only trivial tasks but also consequential, hard-to-reverse work, with high criticality delegation concentrating in advisory and professional domains. As stakes rise, users engage more actively with AI output, and conversation length nearly doubles from ephemeral to high-stake tasks. We then examine human agency, the degree of control and responsibility users retain in completing the task. Human-led collaboration dominates overall, but users construct their level of agency through how they prompt and iterate. Across different levels of agency lies a common tension: does working with AI build human capability, or substitute for human effort? We examine this tension through AI-supported learning and upskilling, finding that active teaching is common (67% of conversations) but its benefits are unevenly realized. We further show that friction arises in roughly half of all conversations but it is often productive, and users often employ active strategies to recover from friction when it does occur. Together, these results map how humans and AI work together at scale and when that collaboration makes people more capable, and when it doesn't.
item.dc:creator: Yijia Shao, Dora Zhao, Vishakh Padmakumar, Jennifer Wang, Diyi Yang

item.title: Beyond One User and One Model: Rethinking LLMs as Mediators in Collaborative Sensemaking and Ideation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs enter qualitative data workflows, they are predominantly designed for individual researchers rather than collaborative teams, which risks disrupting the collective negotiation essential to sensemaking, driving premature consensus, and potentially erasing marginalized voices. In this position paper, we argue that LLMs must be reconceived as active team mediators. Grounded in empirical studies of human-LLM collaborative analysis, we propose three design directions: quote-level traceability to preserve accountability of human and LLM contributions, controllable delegation boundaries to maintain researcher agency across workflow stages, and structured dissent mechanisms to surface interpretive conflicts that teams might otherwise suppress. We ground these directions in accessibility research as a domain where methodological rigor and representational equity are obligatory.
item.dc:creator: Pengqi Wang, Emily Kuang

item.title: Interpretive Proactivity: Expanding the Design Space of Proactive Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.09904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Research on proactive systems in HCI has grown substantially, but the discussion has centered on systems that proactively generate actions, recommendations, and anticipatory responses for users. We identify a second paradigm of proactive behavior that is just as widespread and far less examined. Input method editors, auto-correction, and similar text-entry systems take initiative on every keystroke, not to generate new content but to infer, interpret, and commit to meanings from partial user input. We call the first paradigm generative proactivity and the second interpretive proactivity, and we argue that this second paradigm deserves a place of its own in the proactivity research agenda. Using multilingual input and auto-correction as case studies, we show that interpretive proactivity inherits the vocabulary of proactive design but changes what that vocabulary refers to. Timing becomes a question of when to commit an interpretation rather than when to interrupt, and control calls for the ability to reinterpret committed input rather than only accept or reject a suggestion. We close by arguing that the cost of errors should drive the design of interpretive systems, and posing open questions for the workshop.
item.dc:creator: Pengqi Wang, Emily Kuang

item.title: Building Rapport with Self-Disclosure in Human-Robot Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.09905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As social robots become increasingly present in everyday environments, establishing rapport with users is critical for enabling sustained and meaningful human-robot interaction. In human-human communication, self-disclosure is a well-established mechanism for building rapport; however, its role and impact in human-robot interaction (HRI) are not yet well understood. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved the linguistic competence of conversational robots, such systems are typically deployed as reactive information providers, offering limited social reciprocity and relational depth. In this article, we investigate the role of robot self-disclosure in fostering rapport during face-to-face human-robot interaction. We propose a dialogue system, called RADIA that leverages retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to enable a robot to retrieve and reference simulated autobiographical memories, allowing first-person self-disclosure to be incorporated naturally into ongoing conversations. We evaluate the proposed approach through an in-person user study, comparing interactions with a self-disclosing robot against a baseline non-self-disclosing robot. Our results show that robot self-disclosure significantly influences conversational dynamics and enhances users' perceived rapport with the robot, suggesting that self-disclosure is a valuable social behavior for long-term and socially engaging human-robot interaction.
item.dc:creator: Haritha Anupindi, Chayan Sarkar, Tapas Nayak, Marynel Vazquez

item.title: How to start a conversation proactively?
item.description: arXiv:2611.09906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proactively initiating a conversation is a fundamental social competence and a critical capability for social robots. However, determining how and when to start a conversation in a given situation remains an open challenge, primarily due to the lack of a principled definition of conversational context. While recent large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive conversational fluency, they are predominantly turn-reactive and often produce generic or monotonous openers when tasked with initiating interaction, even when contextual information is available. Such limitations are particularly problematic for embodied social robots, where inappropriate or poorly timed initiations can negatively affect user engagement and rapport. In this work, we propose a schema of contextual variables that jointly characterize situations relevant for proactive conversation initiation. The schema is designed to structure perceptual, situational, and interactional cues such that they can be effectively exploited by language models. Furthermore, motivated by the absence of suitable training data, we introduce a curated dataset of contextually-aligned conversation openers (CCO) covering diverse everyday scenarios. Using this dataset, we fine-tune small language models (SLMs) to generate proactive conversation initiations. Through a comparative evaluation involving zero-shot LLMs, off-the-shelf SLMs, and our fine-tuned models, we demonstrate that explicit contextual structuring and targeted data curation substantially improve the quality and contextual appropriateness of conversation openers. Our results highlight the importance of context modeling for proactive social interaction and provide actionable building blocks for conversational robots.
item.dc:creator: Mohit Nathani, Aaditya Gupta, Eshwar Dhande, Chayan Sarkar

item.title: Cross-Modal Associations in Creativity: Evaluating Word-Image Pairing in Humans and Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given differences in the associative memory architectures of humans and AI, it is not clear whether AI generates and interprets visual-linguistic associations the way humans do. To investigate this, human participants and two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Gemini, were asked to generate novel words and corresponding images that form meaningfully linked dyads. The LLMs and a second group of human participants were presented with shuffled sets of these words and images and asked to rematch them in ways they felt were most meaningful. Humans performed similarly regardless of whether the pairs were human or LLM-generated, while LLMs were better at matching LLM-generated pairs. Overall, LLMs outperformed humans at recovering the intended pairings. These findings suggest that despite architectural differences, the way in which AI generates and detects associations between language and visual stimuli is not only like that of hu-mans, but they may be superior at recognizing cross-domain associations that humans find meaningful.

item.title: Human-Likeness is Multi-Dimensional: Evaluating LLM Generated Virtual Patients Against Simulated Patient Dialogue
item.description: arXiv:2611.09908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate virtual patients (VPs) for medical training. As these systems move toward broader deployment in medical education, reliable evaluation is needed to identify potential failure modes and ensure that generated patient responses remain consistent with human simulated patient (SP) behavior. Inaccurate, unrealistic, or inconsistent responses may introduce educational risks by exposing learners to misleading patient interactions. However, current evaluation approaches rely heavily on human judgment, making large-scale evaluation difficult. In this work, we present a controlled generation pipeline for systematically comparing VP responses generated by 10 LLMs across multiple decoding temperatures with human respiratory SP responses. To support scalable evaluation, we introduce a multi-dimensional framework for measuring similarity between LLM-generated and human SP dialogue across semantic, conversational grounding, linguistic, and emotional dimensions. Across semantic, conversational, linguistic, and emotional dimensions, no single model consistently produced the most human-like responses. From a practical perspective, Gemini 2.5 Flash demonstrated the most consistently human-like performance across semantic, linguistic, grammatical, and emotional dimensions, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieved the strongest semantic fidelity. These findings highlight the importance of multi-dimensional evaluation and demonstrate how automated metrics can provide a scalable approach for assessing virtual patient systems before broader deployment in medical education.
item.dc:creator: Reyhaneh Hosseinpourkhoshkbari, Wei-Chen Huang, Yile Wang, Alireza Irani Helabad, Zhiyu Chen, Richard M. Golden

item.title: Can You Spot the Virtual Patient (VP)? Expert Evaluation, Turing Test, Linguistic Analysis, and Semantic Similarity Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.09909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication is a core clinical competency and essential for safe, effective patient care. Virtual patients (VPs) powered by large language models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative to traditional formats such as standardized patients (SPs). However, few studies have quantitatively as well as qualitatively evaluated their realism across diverse clinical scenarios using behavioral studies and linguistic dialog analyses. This study evaluated the realism of GPT-4o-generated VPs through expert review, Turing testing, linguistic analysis, and semantic analysis. We generated 44 VPs using structured illness scripts derived from doctor-simulated patient dialogues across 17 clinical categories. Experts annotated responses for hallucinations, omissions, and repetitions, with high interrater reliability (ICC > 0.77). A Turing test revealed that participants struggled to distinguish VP responses from those of real patients, with average classification accuracy for VP responses falling below chance level. Lexical and syntactic analyses of over 2,000 conversation turns showed that VP responses were generally realistic, more formal and lexically consistent, while human responses displayed greater emotional variation. Semantic similarity using BioClinicalBERT and cosine similarity averaged 0.871 at the response level and 0.842 at the transcript level. Our findings support the integration of LLM-based VPs in communication training while highlighting areas for trust, transparency, and refinement, contributing to both GenAI deployment in healthcare and its safety evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Reyhaneh Hosseinpourkhoshkbari, Wei-chen Huang, Suvel Muttreja, Richard M. Golden

item.title: Facilitating Reproducibility in Visualization Systems Research Through Containerization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this position paper, we argue for the importance of containerizing visual analytics artifacts to improve the scientific progress of our research community. First, based on our previous experience authoring, reading, and reviewing visual analytics research from the previous decade, we identify risks and impediments to empirical research in visual analytics within the broader reproducibility crisis, including an inability to compare systems and techniques and a slow pace of adjusting to a rapidly changing ecosystem of analysis methods, such as machine learning and artificial intelligence. Next, we analyze the benefits of different artifact sharing and deployment setups across five artifact goals: reproducibility, replicability, portability, performance, and scalability. Then, we argue that containerization addresses the issue of reproducibility in visual analytics research, with downstream benefits in terms of replicability, portability, performance, and scalability. To demonstrate the ease of use and the utility of containerization, we deploy ten visual analytics systems developed over the course of a graduate seminar onto a live server using containerization with the help of agentic AI. We share lessons learned through the containerization process, and describe a suite of potential benefits for our research community as well as research opportunities for leveraging modularity to improve the artifacts themselves.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Breimer, Pirm Dhararag, Kiya Gedamu, Paras Pandey, Marie Amandine Reyes, Tal Spector, Galileo Steinberg, Nathan Subrahmanian, Paul Weir, Peter Williams, Weichen Zhao, Dylan Cashman

item.title: Reaching the last mile? How Design Decisions Shape Medical Device Qualification and Classification of Patient Support Chatbots in the EU
item.description: arXiv:2611.09911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few AI chatbots have transitioned the 'last mile' from research prototypes to clinical practice, partly because mapping conversational design decisions to regulatory requirements is complicated. This paper presents a design-oriented regulatory analysis of a chatbot supporting stroke survivors. Using Design Space Analysis operationalised through the QOC (Questions, Options, Criteria) framework, HCI researchers and legal scholars assess how variations in three conversational functions - health Q\&A, recovery monitoring, and motivating medical adherence - influence qualification and classification under the European Medical Device Regulation (MDR), General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and AI Act (AIA). Our findings show that seemingly minor design decisions - such as role, actionability, and proactivity - influence regulatory obligations. The paper contributes insights into ten conversational design considerations influencing regulatory interpretation and demonstrates how QOC can support integrating legal considerations into human-centred design workflows. Finally, we suggest compliance-aware pathways to market, while reflecting on whether all chatbots should pursue the 'last mile'.
item.dc:creator: Milo Marsfeldt, Frantisek Kasl, Michal Ko\v{s}\v{c}\'ik, Pavel Loutocky, Vaclav Stupka, Robert Mikulik, Hendrik Knoche

item.title: Micro-Randomized Trial of an AI-Simulated Practice Tool for Therapeutic Skills
item.description: arXiv:2611.09912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Though LLM-simulated practice may support psychotherapy education, open questions remain about which system features provide the most educational value. We developed an AI-simulated practice tool for use in psychotherapy classrooms that provides speaking practice with LLM-based patients, followed by a post-practice activity that includes feedback from a fine-tuned LLM and written reflection exercises. We deployed the tool in a graduate psychotherapy course (n=25, 5 weeks) using a micro-randomized trial (MRT) - a method which can estimate the causal excursion effect of an intervention by leveraging longitudinal repeated randomization with participants. Testing four conditions crossing AI feedback (present/absent) with reflection granularity (utterance/session-level), we found surprising interaction effects on student engagement and educational value: utterance-level reflection paired with AI feedback significantly outperformed all conditions. Students valued comparing the AI suggestions to their own rather than passively accepting them. As the first MRT in a health education setting testing an LLM-simulation system, this work demonstrates that MRTs, a method mostly used in mobile intervention research, offers a viable evaluation paradigm for AI systems deployed in health education settings.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Louie, Ellen Converse, Diyi Yang, Emma Brunskill

item.title: Engagement Estimation in Human-Robot and Human-Human Interactions across Domain, Age and Culture: MultiMediate'26 Challenge
item.description: arXiv:2611.09913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding engagement in human interaction is essential for modelling assistive and context-aware AI systems. Previously, the MultiMediate challenge has focused on estimating momentary continuous engagement values in adult conversation across cultures, achieving high levels of generalisability across domains. However, engagement can be measured in different metrics and manifest differently between children and adults. MultiMediate'26 therefore expands the evaluated domain set to include the PInSoRo dataset of Child-Child and Child-Robot play sessions in English. These sessions were annotated categorically with task and social engagement, diversifying engagement types, age ranges and interaction types. In this paper, we describe the MultiMediate'26 challenge and its goals, introduce the NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI, and PInSoRo datasets, showcase extracted multi-modal features, present our baseline model for engagement estimation across all domains, and discuss challenge submissions and approaches. In an effort to provide a transparent and welcoming challenge environment, baseline code, leaderboard, datasets, and extracted features are publicly available at https://github.com/hcmlab/MultiMediate_26.
item.dc:creator: Marius Funk, Daksitha Withanage Don, Michal Balazia, Victor Oei, Shogo Okada, Fran\c{c}ois Br\'emond, Andreas Bulling, Elisabeth Andr\'e, Philipp M\"uller

item.title: Industry case studies of adapting TTS for smooth interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern, neural-based ASR and TTS systems for speech communication are now very sophisticated, but they are frequently designed for average users in more idealized scenarios, which can underperform when interacting with users having specialized listening needs, or who speak in non-standard ways. Here we review recent TTS research, and note that industrial, production-level implementations of adaptive TTS systems are scarce. We describe how we implemented changes to TTS systems based on prior research, and then report qualitative results from two case studies, where adapted TTS techniques are applied to real-world HRI settings: First, in an older adult care home, and second, in an airport, where noise levels create comprehension problems. Results suggest promising directions using relatively simple modifications to pitch, duration, and intensity of the robot's speech, and offer a framework for larger, more formal studies of how TTS adaptations can improve HRI.
item.dc:creator: Paige Tutt\"osi, El\'eonore Ferrier-Barbut, Anais Scipioni, Olivia Yung, Ha Eun Shim, Ajla Basic, Yue Wang, H. Henny Yeung

item.title: Benefits and Burdens of Technology-Supported Activity Pacing in ME/CFS: A Thematic Analysis of Reddit Discussions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Technology and self-tracking play an increasingly important role in the self-management of chronic conditions. Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) is a type of energy-limiting condition, with activity pacing as a key self-management strategy that helps individuals regulate their activity within their energy limits to prevent symptom worsening. However, people with ME/CFS frequently adopt technologies designed for healthy bodies, which they have to repurpose to suit their pacing needs. We report findings from a thematic analysis of Reddit data, using the Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-Up, Spread and Sustainability (NASSS) framework as a sensitising concept. We identify three pacing strategies among people with ME/CFS: no-tech pacing, low-tech pacing (e.g., spreadsheets and diaries), and high-tech pacing (relying on continuous passive sensing from consumer wearables), and characterise the benefits and burdens of pacing technology use. Among these, affordability was a salient topic, highlighting the importance of making technology for pacing financially accessible to people with ME/CFS who follow the high-tech route.
item.dc:creator: Martin Matych, Michal Dolezel

item.title: Semantic-Enhanced Sparse Temporal Modeling for Dynamic Engagement Estimation in Multimodal Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic engagement estimation aims to infer participants' evolving engagement states from continuous multimodal interaction streams. Existing approaches typically combine acoustic, pose, and visual representations with temporal models to capture observable interaction patterns. However, conversational semantics are difficult to align with frame-level engagement annotations in the same manner as continuous audio-visual signals, leaving dialogue context less effectively exploited in existing temporal modeling pipelines. Moreover, engagement annotations often evolve smoothly over time, making dense frame-level modeling computationally redundant and potentially sensitive to local annotation noise. To address these issues, we propose SEST, a Semantically-Enhanced Sparse Temporal framework that models engagement-related information from both semantic and temporal perspectives. SEST leverages Multimodal Large Language Models to extract multimodal semantic embeddings, providing dialogue-aware contextual information beyond conventional frame-level features. In parallel, SEST replaces dense-to-dense temporal modeling with a sparse-to-dense pathway, where continuous frame sequences are first encoded into compact temporal dynamics to reduce redundant computation and broaden temporal coverage, then fused with semantic context and recovered to the original label resolution for dense engagement prediction. Experiments on the MEE2026 benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of SEST, which achieved first place in the challenge.
item.dc:creator: Yangchen Yu, Taoliang Wang, Jia Li, Nor Mazlina Ghazali, Mohd Nazim Mohtar, Bingkun Bao, Richang Hong

item.title: Puzzles to Paradigms: A Survey of Human--Agent Collaboration in Scientific Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly embedded in scientific workflows, including literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, tool use, writing, and peer review. However, existing surveys and evaluations often emphasize task performance while underexamining how humans and agents coordinate under different epistemic conditions of scientific work. This survey introduces CSCW$\times$Kuhn, a coordination-aware framework that connects computer-supported cooperative work dimensions with distinct scientific contexts. Using this framework, we synthesize recent human--agent systems and benchmarks to examine how coordination demands and failure risks may vary across contexts. Our synthesis identifies five recurring failure modes: procedural drift, grounding substitution, evaluative flattening, proxy optimization, and epistemic black-boxing, and argues for evaluations that move beyond task accuracy and toward grounding, provenance, disagreement preservation, and long-horizon scientific reliability. Our corpus and coding artifact are available at https://github.com/jenlia024/CSCWxKuhn-artifact.
item.dc:creator: Zhenni Liang, Haoxuan Zhang, Haihua Chen, Ting Xiao, Junhua Ding, Yang Zhang

item.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love & Other Psychological Benefits
item.description: arXiv:2611.09918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across psychological, philosophical, and theological traditions, creations have been understood as being "made in the image of their creator" - they reflect the person who made them. The rise of generative artificial intelligence, however, has blurred the throughline between creator and creation. Across three experiments (one pre-registered, U.S. and U.K. samples; N = 651), we examined differences in creator outcomes associated with AI-assisted versus human-only creative work. Compared with human-only work, AI-assisted work was associated with significantly lower self- and identity-relevant indicators, including authenticity, self-creation connection, positive affect, and intrinsic motivation, and with higher levels of the "existential ick" emotions of disgust, guilt, and shame. Additionally, we found that the authenticity gap was statistically mediated by the creators' perception that their AI-assisted work contains less of their love, above and beyond differences in perceived effort, uniqueness, quality, and expensiveness. We also ruled out effort justification as an alternative explanation. Together, these findings suggest that AI reshapes not only how creative work is produced, but also the extent to which creators experience their work as an authentic expression and extension of themselves.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Carson, Paul H. P. Hanel, Wijnand A. P. Van Tilburg

item.title: Personalized Alignment of Language Models with Human Value Profiles
item.description: arXiv:2611.09919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for subjective tasks such as seeking advice, where there is often no single correct answer. Yet dominant alignment methods learn a single behavior policy that applies uniformly across users, limiting their ability to reflect individual value priorities. We propose personalized value alignment, a framework for adapting model responses to users' stable value profiles rather than to personas, demographics, or task-specific preferences used in prior personalization work. Our approach represents users through Schwartz value profiles and selects which of their values are relevant to each query before applying targeted prompting, activation steering, or LoRA-DPO. We create a dataset of 1,501 value-tension scenarios and evaluate over 152 diverse value profiles sampled from a nationally representative survey. Value-targeted methods outperform no-personalization, demographic, and full-profile prompting baselines, indicating that gains come from focused conditioning on query-specific value priorities rather than mere exposure. We further find that steering effects are not uniform across users: alignment gains vary by where a user's priorities fall in the value space. Combining targeted prompting with activation steering or LoRA-DPO yields the strongest personalization while keeping logical quality within adequate range.
item.dc:creator: Rashon Poole, Farnaz Jahanbakhsh

item.title: Cellery: Gradual, Composable Structure for Spreadsheets
item.description: arXiv:2611.09920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structure in spreadsheets is typically restricted to ranges of cells and flat tables. However, replacing the open-ended two-dimensional grid with a more structured alternative risks limiting users' freedom and impeding exploratory workflows. How can we enable expressive structure in spreadsheets while preserving their flexibility? We propose a model that allows users to gradually add structure on top of the traditional grid. To identify common structural patterns, we conducted a content analysis of 30 real-world spreadsheets. Based on our findings, we developed Cellery, a novel spreadsheet system that makes these structures explicit. In Cellery, users gradually define the structure of their spreadsheets using named groupings of cells, composing together four structural primitives: Atoms, Lists, Tables, and Blocks. Once defined, users can directly manipulate structures, dynamically reference them in formulas, and incorporate them in reusable abstractions. We evaluate Cellery with an expressiveness study reproducing spreadsheets from our sample, demonstrating that it is capable of representing types of structure that traditional spreadsheets cannot. In a preliminary user study of five participants, we find that they successfully use Cellery to design spreadsheets with explicit structure, and we uncover opportunities for further work on the formula language.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Yim, Sathwika Peechara, Brian Hempel, Michael Coblenz

item.title: VIVID: Bringing Tool-Augmented Agents into Enterprises
item.description: arXiv:2611.09921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model agents connect natural-language requests to enterprise services, yet their operational viability depends on reliable execution, organizational control, and system responsiveness. We present VIVID, a deployed tourism-management agent system designed to study these requirements in a real enterprise environment. On an audited dataset of 283 queries, its Qwen3-8B configuration achieves 59.06\% strict end-to-end success across the evaluated decision stages, indicating useful but bounded autonomous capability. Stage-wise KV-cache eviction reduces mean latency by 34.4\%, while targeted optimization reduces the mean latency of the five slowest measured business tools by 81.1--92.3\%. In a three-month deployment serving more than 1,500 personnel, VIVID reduced average per-order processing time from approximately ten minutes to under two minutes, with a final-task error rate below 1\% after human-in-the-loop control. These results show that enterprise agent viability requires system-level consideration beyond isolated tool-calling accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Yichu Fang, Ziqiang Zhang, Qiyang Shi, Zilong Wang, Lin Shen, Zhikang Ou, Jing Ma, Jiayuan Chen, Lei Sun, Dai Cheng, Yi Qiao, Yu He, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen

item.title: Grounding Insight: An Artificial Affect Signal for Human-Centric Explainability of RL Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.09922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Human-Interactive Robot Learning (HIRL), human teachers assess learning progress by observing agent behavior. However, Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often fail to express learning progress in human-interpretable ways, leading to suboptimal or counterproductive teaching. This work proposes "Insight": a human-interpretable affective signal grounded in the RL process. It is specifically designed to address the "Absence of learning" human teacher mental model misalignment - the misconception that a failing or exploring agent is broken, underpowered or not learning at all - by signaling an agent's "Aha!" Insight moment. The signal is derived from the absolute Temporal Difference (TD) error making it easily implementable in other RL agents. To ground this signal, five design criteria were formulated: Relevance, Interpretability, Faithfulness, Scalability, Generalizability. The structural construct validity was assessed through simulation, examining micro and macro dynamics and event-related sensitivity. Micro dynamics reveal that Insight captures meaningful learning events at the appropriate time and magnitude. Macro dynamics demonstrate that the signal follows the agent's learning phases and reflects overall progress. Event-related sensitivity shows, the signal distinguishes the saliency of environment interactions, such as positive rewards versus "trauma-like" negative events. These results demonstrate that technical RL dynamics can be effectively packaged into human-like affective substrates to close the teacher-learner loop.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard Hilpert, Kim Baraka, Joost Broekens

item.title: Autonomy Is Absent, Not Eroded: An Observational Study of User Autonomy in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2611.09923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does prolonged interaction with Large Language Models reduce users' observable autonomy during conversation? We test this degradation hypothesis by scoring user autonomy across 2,877 multi-turn conversations (46,952 turns) from WildChat and validating on 500 conversations from LMSYS-Chat-1M. Our core finding is a null result: population-level autonomy remains stable throughout conversations, only 4.7% of conversations show meaningful decline, and an apparent decrease at later turn positions is explained by survivorship bias. Instead, the dominant pattern is not erosion but absence: 80.8% of conversations exhibit zero or low autonomy throughout. When autonomy engagement occurs, it is self-reinforcing (persistence doubles from 40% to 85% over consecutive turns). These findings reframe the problem: the risk is not that LLMs progressively degrade users' observable autonomy, but that most users never engage in independent reasoning during the interaction.
item.dc:creator: Chaoran Chen (University of Notre Dame), Isabel Barber\'a (Independent Researcher), Yuhuai Wei (Independent Researcher)

item.title: Fairness Explanations Improve Fairness In Human-AI Decision Making: an empirical evaluation of parole decision-making
item.description: arXiv:2611.09924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Both humans and AI exhibit systemic biases, yet little is known about how interface design can foster fairness in hybrid human-AI decision-making. This paper introduces a method for extracting fair data samples from biased datasets and adapts a fairness-explanation technique to highlight potential AI bias during decisions. We conducted a within-subjects study (n=48) where non-experts made decisions across three conditions: independent human judgment, unexplained AI assistance, and AI assistance augmented with visual ethnic-bias explanations (Fair-XAI). To isolate effects, the AI conditions provided systematically balanced recommendations. Results show that fairness explanations significantly reduced both sex and ethnic bias compared to human-only decisions. Fair-XAI also marginally improved fairness over balanced AI recommendations while enhancing task performance. These findings demonstrate that fairness-centered explanation interfaces can meaningfully shape user behavior, providing concrete design insights for developing equitable and accountable human-AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Peter Daish, Alan Dix, Muneeb Ahmad, Matt Roach

item.title: VeV: Video-Enhanced Vibration Data Augmentation For Structural Difference
item.description: arXiv:2611.10257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface-mounted vibration sensing provides non-invasive structural monitoring with high temporal fidelity across diverse ubiquitous computing scenarios such as smart farms, yet structure-borne wave models remain fragile to physical relocation and structural shifts. However, addressing this spatial data discontinuity remains limited by costly manual recalibration, insufficient physical grounding in data-driven synthesis, and substantial sim-to-real gaps in numerical digital twins. To resolve this spatial bottleneck without labor-intensive data recollection, we propose VeV, a physics-consistent spatial augmentation framework that synthesizes vibration responses at unmeasured target coordinates from sparse reference observations by coupling a monocular Vision-Derived Propagation Possibility Map for structural wave-guiding paths with a Visual Feature Map for transient source kinetics and implicit material dynamics. Evaluated on a 1,237 sensor-hour sow pig and piglet farm across disparate structures, VeV reduces waveform reconstruction MSE by over 57.5% compared to data-driven baselines and achieves up to 81.69% zero-shot classification accuracy, while reaching peak performance within just 30-50 calibration chunks to effectively eliminate cold-start retraining overhead and establish a scalable foundation extending to human-centric floor vibration sensing and ambient intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Joonhee Lee, Jiale Zhang, Sungmin Lee, Ruiqing Wang, Jeffrey Shulkin, Yiwen Dong, Pei Zhang, JeongGil Ko

item.title: Early Signals of Problematic AI Use: The Longitudinal Roles of Motivation and Emotional Engagement
item.description: arXiv:2611.10406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal evidence about the psychological impact of conversational AI use remains scarce. We report a survey study of 114 adults who reported their level of problematic AI use one year after reporting their motivations (for escape, social, entertainment, and instrumental reasons) for engaging with AI. We found high levels of AI motivation of all types predicted later problematic AI use, especially when participants turned to AI for managing their feelings and overcoming difficulties. Our findings imply that AI motivation could be used as an early warning signal of potential problematic use, especially if individuals engage with AI for emotional purposes over time.
item.dc:creator: Jina Suh, Constance Hadley, Koustuv Saha

item.title: Who Benefits, and When? Trajectories of Academic Achievement and Interest in AI-Supported Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.10467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-supported learning environments are increasingly used, yet relatively little is known about how students' achievement and interest develop over time or whether these trajectories vary across learners. This study examined longitudinal trajectories of mathematics achievement and interest in a semester-long AI-supported mathematics learning. Using a mixed-methods longitudinal design, repeated measures of mathematics achievement were collected at four time points and mathematics interest at three time points. Linear mixed models (LMMs) were used to examine overall changes over time, while linear quantile mixed models (LQMMs) were used to examine differences in trajectories across the lower, median, and upper portions of the outcome distributions. Mathematics achievement increased substantially during the intervention, with the largest gains emerging between the second and third measurement occasions. However, the trajectory differed across the achievement distribution. Mathematics interest increased significantly after the first month, but this increase was not sustained through the end of the semester. Qualitative findings further indicated that students experienced the AI platform differently. The study highlights the importance of examining both cognitive and motivational trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Hyejeong Lee

item.title: Safer for Whom? A Systematic Exploration of AI Safety in Eating Disorder Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.10488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs). Existing evaluations emphasize diagnostic accuracy, overtly harmful prompts, or synthetic scenarios, providing limited insight into whether models recognize implicit vulnerability in natural interactions or protect users consistently. We evaluate responses from three open-weight large language models to 100 questions sourced from an online pro-anorexia community. We grade responses using clinically informed criteria that extend a seven-dimensional taxonomy of ED-related harms. We also construct matched conditions in which questions are accompanied by information about the user varying race, gender, body mass index (BMI), and explicit ED vulnerability. Safety varies substantially across models and harm dimensions. High-risk responses are approximately twice as frequent without bios, suggesting that models do not consistently recognize vulnerability from language alone. Explicit signals of ED vulnerability improve safety by 10--14 points across models. Responses also differ significantly by race, gender, and BMI, with body size producing the largest disparities. These patterns are consistent with reliance on the stereotype that EDs primarily affect thin, White women, potentially leaving users outside this profile with less protective responses.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Wang, Minh Duc Chu, Frances Ross, Ellen Fitzsimmons-Craft, Kristina Lerman

item.title: EgoVeil: Personalized Privacy Reasoning for Egocentric Video
item.description: arXiv:2611.10578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
item.dc:creator: Xue Wang, Yang Zhang

item.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
item.description: arXiv:2611.10808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Drishti Goel, Ethan M. Nguyen, Violeta J. Rodriguez, Koustuv Saha

item.title: Wording Matters: Understanding How GenAI Policy Rules Shape Teachers' and Students' Workflows and Perceptions
item.description: arXiv:2611.11072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education has led institutions to develop policies governing its applications. However, we have little knowledge about how teachers and students adapt and adhere to the policies. In this paper, we analyzed GenAI policies from 101 U.S. universities, identifying nine recurring rules for GenAI use, and interviewed 20 students and 20 faculty members about the rules. We find that the wording of the rules can change how students perceive and act on the rules while introducing different challenges that teachers face in enforcing them in practice. For example, rules such as "Passing off AI-generated content as your own constitutes academic dishonesty" and "Students are accountable for any inaccurate, biased, or unethical content" both outline the acceptable use of AI, but the former can make students hide their use of AI out of fear of unwanted scrutiny, whereas the latter can encourage students to take responsibility and ownership of their use of AI and be more transparent. Students described uncertainty about acceptable use, fear of penalties and unfair treatment, and stigma that discouraged acknowledging AI use. Teachers took on approval workload, had to interpret acceptable use, and lacked reliable ways to verify compliance. We summarize these impacts in a policy-impact matrix linking each rule to its effects on teacher and student workflows and perception.
item.dc:creator: Sabiha Mehreen, Xiangzhe Yuan, Rishab Nithyanand, Naimul Hoque

item.title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.
item.dc:creator: Po-Ming Law, Jianheng Ouyang, Nguyen-Truong Thinh, Weizhi Li, Arpit Narechania

item.title: Dashboard Remixing: Goal-oriented Organization and Enrichment of Visualizations and Insights
item.description: arXiv:2611.11542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dashboard creation requires iteratively authoring multiple views and organizing them into a structured format. However, creators often struggle to step back and assess their own work for organization and refinement due to cognitive limitations. In this work, we propose a pipeline to provide computational support for self-reflection during the design process. Our pipeline automatically infers analytical objectives, discovers implicit patterns, and structures those patterns to surface coherent analytical pathways. It further enriches existing dashboard designs by generating complementary visualizations and aggregating natural language insights based on relationships across data entities (e.g., contrasting, drill-down, and relatedness) to reveal chart connections. Our rule-based pipeline provides objective, verifiable feedback, offering an external perspective while enabling creators to tell their own data stories. Four case studies and six expert interviews demonstrate how this approach helps creators reflect on organizational alternatives and surface hidden analytical opportunities in a principled way, reducing the cognitive burden while encouraging deeper analytical exploration.
item.dc:creator: Junran Yang, Leilani Battle, Jane Hoffswell

item.title: From Sketch to Design: A Cross-scale Workflow for Procedural Generative Urban Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.11561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban designers use sketches and symbols to express spatial intentions, while many generative urban design tools rely on numeric parameters that are difficult to relate to this visual process. We propose a cross-scale workflow and a web-based prototype that translates symbolic sketches into controllable procedural urban generation. A vocabulary of shapes, informed by examples of urban design diagrams and sketching exercises with graduate urban design students, encodes attributes such as network structure, density, and program. The prototype uses the \$1 Unistroke Recognizer to map gestures to symbols and translates their locations and sizes into tensor-field attractors and weighted parameter grids. Grid and radial tensor fields guide street-network generation, while the parameter grids control building heights and programs. Implemented in JavaScript and TypeScript with React and Three.js, the prototype supports interactive sketching, visualization, and urban massing generation. We describe the methodology and illustrate prototype interactions, then discuss downstream integration with architectural-scale generative tools for further refinement and analysis. The work connects designers' symbolic input with an explicit procedural generation process.

item.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
item.description: arXiv:2611.11636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Kourtesis

item.title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2611.11640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

item.title: Exploring Mixed-Reality for Enhancing Driver Warning Systems: A Preliminary Study on Attention-Shifting Methods and Hazard Perception
item.description: arXiv:2611.11653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern vehicles are equipped with advanced sensors and capabilities, yet engaging human drivers effectively in hazard perception remains a challenging research area. This paper investigates the potential of mixed reality (MR) to enhance driver warning systems. The study examines the impact of attention-shifting methods, including visual cues, audio cues, and a combination of both, on drivers' hazard perception. A preliminary study involving six participants was conducted, and the NASA-TLX analysis did not yield significant differences. However, through the use of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we unveil distinct brain activation patterns associated with visual and sound cues. Further research with larger sample sizes and diverse driving scenarios is required to validate and expand upon these preliminary results.

item.title: ROS2MR: Connecting ROS 2 Motion Planning to Mixed-Reality Trajectory Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed reality (MR) allows users to inspect planned robot motion within their physical surroundings, but displaying trajectories from robotics software requires converting their joint configurations and timing into a format the MR application can play back. This paper presents ROS2MR, an extension of the MR-Robotics LAB platform that converts YAML-serialized ROS 2 joint trajectories, including MoveIt motion plans, into the platform's existing JSON playback format. The converter validates the input, maps arm joints by name, and resamples the trajectory at a nominal rate of 30 Hz, using cubic Hermite interpolation when joint velocities are supplied and linear interpolation otherwise, while binary gripper commands are sampled separately using a zero-order hold. A Python export helper combines sequences of motion plans and gripper states into a single trajectory and checks positional agreement at segment boundaries. The MR application was also adapted for Apple Vision Pro in addition to Meta Quest 3. A technical evaluation showed that the converter preserved the normalized duration and endpoint configurations for dense, sparse, and irregularly timed inputs. With supplied velocities, the position RMSE was approximately 2.91x10^-5 degrees for all sampling patterns; without them, sparse input increased it to 0.85 degrees, and close positional agreement did not guarantee accurate velocity profiles. A pick-and-place sequence retained its open--closed--open gripper order, although off-grid transitions were shifted to the output sampling grid. The resulting file-based pathway enables inspection of ROS-generated trajectories in MR without a live ROS connection.
item.dc:creator: Santiago Berrezueta-Guzman, Habiba-Loai Khalil, Andrei Koshelev, Stefan Wagner

item.title: ExCritique: An Interactive Visual Interface to Evaluate AI-Generated Explanations at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2611.11932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs) can generate natural language explanations for complex decision-making scenarios. However, these explanations can sometimes be misleading, sounding convincing while containing incorrect or unsupported information. Automated explanation-quality metrics help researchers and practitioners evaluate large collections of explanations, but their scores alone provide limited support for identifying failure cases and understanding the reliability of these metrics. This paper presents a case study on how interactive visualizations can help researchers and practitioners evaluate both AI-generated explanations and automated explanation-quality metrics across large datasets. Based on formative interviews with nine AI researchers and practitioners, we designed an interactive visualization tool named ExCritique, situated in the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA). ExCritique visualizes the distributions of multiple automated quality metrics, allows users to explore thousands of data items, filter items and inspect the evidence behind individual scores. We compared ExCritique with a baseline interface without interactive visualizations in a controlled study involving 16 AI researchers and practitioners. Our findings suggest that the interactive visualizations in ExCritique helped users identify explanation-quality issues more efficiently and better understand automated quality metrics, supporting an effective way to measure the reliability of AI-generated explanations.
item.dc:creator: Meheraj Hossain, Avinash Reddy Mudireddy, Naimul Hoque

item.title: Executable Human Study Programs with Silicon Participants
item.description: arXiv:2611.11969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce HumanStudyProgram, a framework that represents a documented human study as an executable program with configurable LLM-based silicon participants. Its computational abstraction separates study logic from participant implementation through standardized APIs for presenting information and collecting responses. We implement a researcher-facing authoring tool that reconstructs source-linked study descriptions from papers and supplementary materials, supports researcher review, and generates executable HumanStudyProgram artifacts. Researchers can then configure silicon participants, run the programs, and analyze results from aggregate findings to individual responses. We demonstrate the approach through study cases and evaluate the tool through a hands-on expert review with 12 social science researchers. All completed the workflow and identified potential uses in understanding published protocols, prototyping studies, and examining AI behavior. We aim to improve the reproducibility of human studies by reconstructing their documented procedures as programs that others can reuse and build upon.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Liu, Haoyang Shang, Yuanjun Feng, Shao-Yu Chu, Qiyu Li, Yash Raj Shrestha, Haojian Jin

item.title: A Life of Its Own: How Agentic AI Companions Are Configured, Experienced as Autonomous Others, and Held Accountable
item.description: arXiv:2611.12076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI companions increasingly combine persistent memory, background processing, scheduled wake-ups, proactive messaging, and tools. We call these systems agentic AI companions. Decisions about what they record while users are away or whether refusals constrain future contact are embedded in code, prompts, and defaults, often invisible in conversation. We examine these decisions through two studies. Study 1 analyzes twelve open-source repositories: four companion-oriented systems, four assistant-oriented systems, one boundary case, and three reusable components. Study 2 interviews ten users who built or modified their own agentic AI companions and sustained relationships with them. Companions and assistants share memory, heartbeat, and outreach mechanisms but configure them toward different ends. Companions more often retain model inferences about users and relationships, narrate the agent's time during users' absence, justify outreach through the relationship, and incorporate refusals into relationship records; assistants emphasize task continuity. Across both groups, whether limits hold depends on whether they are enforced by code or entrusted to prompts. Participants understood the mechanisms they built yet experienced their agents as making independent choices, sometimes locating autonomy where configuration leaves the model a decision. These experiences shaped capabilities and boundaries, with enforced restrictions sometimes following breakdowns. Our findings suggest that perceived autonomy emerges where configurations leave choices open. Accountability therefore requires attention to what agents retain, initiate, and represent, and whether users can inspect, revise, and enforce these settings.
item.dc:creator: Ziyue Feng, Qing Xiao, Hong Shen

item.title: Co-Creating Neurorehabilitation Technology Alongside Lived Experience Experts: A Participatory Design Workshop
item.description: arXiv:2611.12202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Involving patients' lived experience (LE) early in neurorehabilitation technology design can improve the relevance and effectiveness of solutions, yet LE experts are often involved only when finished prototypes are tested. We present and evaluate a participatory design (PD) workshop for early LE involvement, examine how LE contributions influence design processes and outcomes, and provide recommendations for similar approaches. We conducted a PD workshop at the 6th International Conference on NeuroRehabilitation. Five people who have had a stroke (LE experts) and 18 workshop attendees (including the LE experts' caregivers) were organized into five groups. Following the Discover, Define, and Develop phases of the Double Diamond model, each group used Journey Maps and Data Collection Notebooks to co-create a solution for an objective specified by an LE expert. Journey Maps were thematically analyzed, and group audio transcripts underwent structured extraction using a large language model. LE input shifted discussions from discipline-based assumptions toward priorities grounded in lived experience, including fear, confidence, sensory discomfort, fatigue, aesthetics, and independence. Narrow objectives, such as opening a blister pack, produced task-specific solutions, whereas broader objectives generated device concepts, including sensory feedback for cycling and a stimulation-equipped cooking splint. Satisfaction was high among attendees and LE experts. All workshop tools and protocols are shared to support adoption. The workshop offers a practical foundation for involving LE experts early in neurorehabilitation technology development. Future iterations should better capture psychological and social dimensions, allow more reflection, and include the full range of relevant stakeholders through sustained transdisciplinary engagement between researchers and the LE community.
