item.title: From LLM Hallucinations to Inspiration in Creative Work
item.description: arXiv:2611.12337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can introduce unexpected ideas through hallucinations, yet little is known about when creative practitioners find these errors inspiring or how these judgments shape interactions. We conducted a retrospective qualitative study with 20 experienced practitioners in research, design, and social media content creation, thematically analyzing 41 hallucination cases and 20 semi-structured interviews. Our framework links inspiration judgments of hallucinations based on goal relevance, task stage, content adaptability, and type-specific factors to behaviors across not-inspired, inspired-by, and inspired-to states. We characterize downstream interaction consequences, showing how hallucination-inspired experiences vary across creative stages and reshape role-differentiated trust, and propose these consequences as a dimension of hallucination evaluation. Finally, we derive design recommendations for stage-sensitive control of divergence and adherence, user-defined constraint priorities, differentiated hallucination labels, and salvage support for preserving useful ideas while correcting errors. These contributions deepen HCI understanding of hallucinations and responsible LLM design in creative work.
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Lin, Heyan Huang, Shuning Zhang, Qi Wang, Youchao Zhou, John Vines

item.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
item.description: arXiv:2611.12529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Zhang, Anthony Steed

item.title: Creative Intent as an Evolving Shared State: Supporting Cross-Stage Human-AI Video Co-Creation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly involved in video creation, creators face challenges in expanding, translating, and negotiating creative intent across stages. We therefore view creative intent as an evolving shared state throughout human-AI co-creation. A multi-stage design was employed: semi-structured interviews with 12 creators informed 3 design goals, followed by expert co-design and the development of VideoMaker. VideoMaker organizes creation into a six-stage workflow that progressively translates creative intent. At key stages, creators negotiate with AI through the Seed Panel, explicitly confirming, revising, and updating intent. A shared AI Agent, supported by the Multi-style Script Library and Cinematic Language Knowledge Base, enables differentiated expansion of initial intent and faithful translation. A within-subjects study with 30 participants showed that VideoMaker effectively supported the expansion and cross-stage translation of creative intent, with stronger intent preservation, while negotiated boundaries between creator-confirmed intent and AI initiative remained difficult to sustain.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Jin, Mengfei Chen, Hanwei Zheng, Songruoyao Wu, Kejun Zhang

item.title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.
item.dc:creator: Susie S. Y. Li, Angie Boggust, Fred Hohman, Donghao Ren, Dominik Moritz, Yannick Assogba

item.title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
item.description: arXiv:2611.12834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Priya Dhawka, Benjamin Wilson, Andrew Head

item.title: Why Today's Internet Cannot Support Tomorrow's Immersive Experiences: Insights from the NSF Workshop
item.description: arXiv:2611.09926v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Immersive computing is poised to become a major paradigm for future human-computer interaction (HCI), enabling spatial and embodied experiences across applications such as education, healthcare, manufacturing, emergency response, and scientific discovery. However, today's Internet and computing infrastructure were not designed for real-time, multi-user, sensor-rich, and privacy-sensitive immersive applications. They require coordination across sensing, representation, compression, networking, edge/cloud computing, rendering, security/privacy, and human experience. This report summarizes key findings from the NSF Workshop on Networking and Systems Challenges in Immersive Computing. The workshop brought together researchers from networking, systems, extended reality (XR), artificial intelligence (AI), graphics, HCI, security, privacy, and applications to identify challenges and opportunities. We conclude that immersive computing cannot be enabled by isolated advances in network bandwidth, device capabilities, AI models, or rendering alone. The field needs end-to-end architectures that adapt to user behavior, application requirements, resource constraints, and social expectations. We organize the agenda into six themes: networked systems for immersive computing; real-time edge-cloud orchestration for XR applications; AI for immersive experiences; privacy, security, and trust in XR systems; human-centered design and user experience in XR; and scalable infrastructure, testbeds, and open ecosystems for XR. We further identify key research questions, future trends, risks, ten-year success metrics, and action items for academia, industry, government, and research community. The report calls for coordinated investment in open platforms, reproducible benchmarks, privacy-preserving systems, and human-centered evaluation to build trustworthy, scalable, and broadly impactful infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Bo Han, Amitabh Varshney, Klara Nahrstedt, Songqing Chen, Sarita Adve, Ruofei Du, Xueyu Hou, Yongjie Guan, Jiayi Meng, Qiao Jin, Xiaonan Guo, Nan Wu, Ruizhi Cheng

item.title: Generative Active Learning for Label-Efficient Pan-Organ Ultrasound Diagnosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.10180v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical ultrasound (US) enables real-time, non-invasive diagnosis, yet building US-based AI systems is limited by data scarcity, costly expert annotation, and limited cross-center generalizability. Privacy constraints and instance-level reporting hinder the collection of diverse abnormal cases and frame-level labels, while repeated retraining for new centers increases computational cost. We introduce EvoDiff, a generative active learning framework that integrates diffusion modelling with information-theoretic objectives, evolutionary search, and curriculum-based sampling to select informative samples across heterogeneous US datasets. EvoDiff formulates sample selection as a generate-to-retrieve process, in which diffusion-based optimization in feature space guided by information gain produces synthetic probes, and only the real unlabeled samples retrieved by these probes are annotated and used for downstream training. Across six benchmarks covering fifteen datasets and 16,696 images, we evaluate EvoDiff on convolutional network and transformer-based foundation model. EvoDiff approaches fully supervised performance with substantially fewer labels, outperforms active learning baselines, and improves foundation model generalization under cross-domain external validation on unseen cohorts. A reader study with six radiologists indicates the potential to support clinical annotation workflows, with a model-based estimated 24% to 84% reduction in annotation workload at matched downstream performance.
item.dc:creator: Yaofei Duan, Yuhao Huang, Yuan Gao, Ruixiang Qi, Tianyu Zhang, Yanlin Geng, Yue Sun, Sio-Kei Im, Dong Ni, Dong Xu, Ritse Mann, Tao Tan

item.title: Who Taught the Robot That? Removing One User's Corrections from a Robot Policy That Learns Online
item.description: arXiv:2611.10280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A robot that keeps learning after deployment is corrected by several people in turn, and one of them may later ask to be removed. We show that whether the robot can forget that person depends on how people correct it. The goal of removal is the robot that would exist if the person had never been there, which we compute exactly in two simulated tasks with scripted users. When users correct the robot by taking over control, an ordered log of training updates is enough: retraining on the remaining sessions in their original order gives a robot as close to the goal as training noise allows. Deleting the person's data and retraining in one pass does not, even when the other users' corrections do not depend on the removed person, because it loses the order of training. When users only nudge the robot's action, the other users' corrections carry the removed person's influence, and no method we tested recovers the goal robot. Continuing to train without the person removes most of their habits, but not what their data in the training buffer keep alive. The log can identify one clearly harmful user, but not rank users by influence better than counting their corrections.
item.dc:creator: Eshika Pathak, Leela Krishna

item.title: Collaboration Signatures: Tracking Long-Horizon Dynamics of Cross-Meeting Collaboration Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.10341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enterprise platforms have received increasing attention as a core component of social networks and the Web. However, existing work mostly relies on fragmented logs of small units of work, like emails and chats, and focuses on who connects with whom without sufficient account of collaboration content and dynamics. This work systematically explores tracking collaborations across sequences of meetings as a new approach to interpreting their long-horizon dynamics. Linking 45,426 meetings in a large multinational technology company based on full transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items, we establish a cross-meeting collaboration network of 6,065 collaborations. The network recovers the natural shapes of workplace collaborations: meetings, as snapshots of ongoing collaboration, link into largely tree-shaped structures, while the work content forms nested directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Further, we explore how these networks evolve over time, examining three established perspectives: task division, team composition, and temporal continuity. Each explains part of the dynamics but does not capture the distinctness of long-horizon workplace collaboration: e.g., work flows in a consistent direction between a few pairs of subjects, yet a collaboration's subject explains little of how its meetings are conducted. Instead, accumulating the agenda, interaction, and language of meetings along each tree yields a signature of the collaboration, a distinctive profile that picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. The signature models collaboration better than team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting. We discuss the implications of these cross-meeting dynamics for designing office applications and support tools, and call for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over their long horizon.
item.dc:creator: Shengqi Zhu, Sheshera Mysore, Bahareh Sarrafzadeh

item.title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
item.description: arXiv:2611.10628v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.
item.dc:creator: Yihuang Kang, Pei-Cing Huang, Chan-Tung Ku, Chan Hsu, Pei-Ju Lee, I-Ling Cheng

item.title: Complementarity without ground truth?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10893v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Ferrario, Alessandro Facchini, Federico Cabitza

item.title: Patchbay: a block model for the sonification of ADS-B aircraft data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Patchbay is a design for turning the data that an ADS-B receiver collects into sound by wiring typed blocks together. ADS-B reports are the position and altitude messages that aircraft broadcast and that a small ground receiver can collect. We first describe what such a receiver reports: signals that differ in shape (continuous, stepped, circular, categorical), in resolution, in who produces them, and in how long they stay put, which runs from about ten seconds to the whole time an aircraft is in view. From this we derive a small model. Four kinds of connection carry an aircraft set, a value, an event or audio, and 27 blocks select aircraft, read fields, decide when a note starts, shape values and make sound. One of these blocks makes the receiver act as a radar: scanning by bearing it is a line that rotates about the receiver, and scanning by range it is a ring that grows from the centre or shrinks inward. Each aircraft sounds at the moment the scan reaches it, and the scan's period is set in bars of a beat clock. The model does not depend on a browser. Our reference implementation is a browser editor, contained in one HTML file, that replays two recorded captures and records both an audio take and a MIDI take, a file of the notes played rather than of the sound. We say what is not built and place the work beside the closest systems we found, among them a radar-sweep sequencer for tangible objects from 2006 and a range-ring sonification of ADS-B aircraft published in 2026. Sweeps that trigger sound, and typed connections, both exist in earlier systems. To our knowledge, none of the sources we reached carries the aircraft in view, with every field attached, as one kind of connection in an editor.
item.dc:creator: Arquimedes Canedo

item.title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine
item.description: arXiv:2611.11064v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
item.dc:creator: Piero Molino, Patrick John Chia, Federico Bianchi, Jonathan P. Chen, Paul Szerlip

item.title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
item.description: arXiv:2611.11083v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with similar newcomers who did not, matched on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.
item.dc:creator: Yubo Zhou, Pengyu Chen, Ceren Budak

item.title: From Dialogue to Task: How Cognitive Engagement With Generative Artificial Intelligence Relates to Post-Dialogue Activity and Task Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2611.11435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Zhuang, Aneesha Bakharia, Dragan Ga\v{s}evi\'c, Hassan Khosravi

item.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
item.description: arXiv:2611.11519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nystr\"om-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Both algorithms were scored against twenty 26-s GazeBase reading recordings hand-classified by three trained raters, and each change was reverted in turn. FKM agreed better than MNH as MNH was used: saccade Cohen's kappa rose on all 20 recordings (median +0.034), and saccade boundaries moved from 2-3 ms late to the raters' sample. One change produced this: centring the filter, which removes a three-sample delay. Reinstating the delay returned FKM's saccade kappa to MNH's value, and centring MNH's filter alone made MNH match FKM on saccades and exceed it on post-saccadic events. The position-based test changed how saccades with several velocity peaks were divided, splitting 8% of rater-labelled "wavy" saccades into a saccade and a spurious oscillation against 39% for delay-corrected MNH. FKM's higher post-saccadic velocity floor traded recall for precision. The remaining changes had no measurable effect on these recordings. FKM's improvement over MNH is therefore a filter-alignment correction that MNH users can apply directly, plus a segmentation rule for multi-peak saccades.
item.dc:creator: Lee Friedman, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Oleg Komogortsev

item.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
item.description: arXiv:2611.12750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Sharma, Kelly Marchisio, Kenton Murray, Ziang Xiao

item.title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
item.description: arXiv:2611.12814v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.

item.title: EvolveCaptions: Empowering DHH Users Through Real-Time Collaborative Captioning
item.description: arXiv:2510.02181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often struggle to accurately transcribe speech from Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) speakers. Existing personalization approaches typically require substantial pre-recorded datasets and burden DHH users. We present EvolveCaptions, a collaborative, error-driven personalization system that connects caption correction with speaker-specific ASR adaptation. When transcribing a DHH speaker's speech, hearing partners repair transcription errors, and the system generates short, targeted clauses for the DHH speaker to record. These samples are used to incrementally fine-tune the model. In a study with 12 DHH and six hearing participants, EvolveCaptions reduced Word Error Rate (WER) across five scripted reading rounds, requiring an average of five minutes of additional speech recording. Participants found the interfaces usable but considered recording and correction effortful; acceptability depended on context and anticipated long-term benefit. These findings show the potential of collaborative, cumulative adaptation while exposing the labor and conditions needed to sustain it.
item.dc:creator: Liang-Yuan Wu, Dhruv Jain

item.title: Facilitating the Integration of LLMs Into Online Experiments With Simple Chat
item.description: arXiv:2511.19123v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly prevalent, understanding human-LLM interactions is emerging as a central priority in psychological research. Online experiments offer an efficient means to study human-LLM interactions, yet integrating LLMs into established survey platforms remains technically demanding, particularly when aiming for ecologically realistic, real-time conversational experiences with strong experimental control. We introduce Simple Chat, an open-source, research-focused chat interface that streamlines LLM integration for platforms such as Qualtrics, oTree, and LimeSurvey, while presenting a unified participant experience across conditions. Simple Chat connects to both commercial providers and open-weights models, displays streamed responses incrementally, and offers an administrative interface for fine-grained control of prompts and interface features. Simple Chat is available both as a hosted service that requires no installation and as open-source software that researchers can deploy on their own server or adapt to their needs. By reducing technical barriers and standardizing interfaces, Simple Chat helps advance the study of human-LLM interaction. In this article, we outline Simple Chat's key features, provide a step-by-step tutorial, and demonstrate its utility through two illustrative case studies.
item.dc:creator: R. Bermudez Schettino, A. Dasmeh, L. Brinkmann

item.title: Elsewise: Authoring Open-ended Interactive Narrative with Possibility Space Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2601.15295v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interactive narrative (IN) authors craft spaces of divergent narrative possibilities for players to explore, with the player's input determining which narrative possibilities they actually experience. Generative AI can enable new forms of IN by improvisationally expanding on pre-authored content in response to open-ended player input. However, this extrapolation risks widening the gap between author-envisioned and player-experienced stories, potentially limiting the strength of plot progression and the communication of the author's narrative intent. To bridge the gap, we introduce Elsewise: an authoring tool for LLM-based INs that implements a novel Bundled Storyline concept to enhance author's perception and understanding of the narrative possibility space, allowing authors to explore similarities and differences between possible playthroughs of their IN in terms of open-ended, user-configurable narrative dimensions. A user study (n=12) shows that our approach improves author anticipation of player-experienced narrative, leading to more effective control and exploration of the narrative possibility spaces.
item.dc:creator: Yi Wang, John Joon Young Chung, Melissa Roemmele, Yuqian Sun, Tiffany Wang, Shm Garanganao Almeda, Brett A. Halperin, Yuwen Lu, Max Kreminski

item.title: Visual Affect Analysis: Predicting Emotions of Image Viewers with Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.00123v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for large-scale affect inference from images, but their alignment with human affective ratings remains unclear. We benchmarked 16 proprietary and open-source VLMs on three validated affective image datasets: the International Affective Picture System, the Nencki Affective Picture System, and the Library of AI-Generated Affective Images. In a zero-shot setting, models performed two tasks: (i) top-emotion classification and (ii) prediction of human ratings on 1--7/9 Likert scales for discrete emotions and affective dimensions. We also evaluated rater-conditioned prompting on the LAI-GAI dataset using de-identified participant metadata. Best models showed strong discrete emotion classification (60%--80% on six-emotion tasks; 60%--75% on a 12-category task), with anger and surprise predicted least accurately. For continuous ratings, models aligned moderately to strongly with human judgments ($r > 0.75$) but showed consistent biases, especially weaker performance on arousal and overestimation of response intensity. Rater-conditioned prompting had only small, inconsistent effects. Overall, VLMs captured broad affective patterns but sometimes lacked the nuance, although newer model generations performed better.
item.dc:creator: Filip Nowicki, Hubert Marciniak, Jakub {\L}\k{a}czkowski, Bartosz Wilczek, Krzysztof Jassem, Tomasz G\'orecki, Vimala Balakrishnan, Desmond C. Ong, Maciej Behnke

item.title: VACP: Visual Analytics Context Protocol
item.description: arXiv:2603.29322v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rise of AI agents introduces a fundamental shift in Visual Analytics (VA), in which agents act as a new user group. Current agentic approaches - based on computer vision and raw DOM access - fail to perform VA tasks accurately and efficiently. This paper introduces the Visual Analytics Context Protocol (VACP), a framework designed to make VA applications "agent-ready" that extends generic protocols by explicitly exposing application state, available interactions, and mechanisms for direct execution. To support our context protocol, we contribute a formal specification of AI agent requirements and knowledge representations in VA interfaces. We instantiate VACP as a library compatible with major visualization grammars and web frameworks, enabling augmentation of existing systems and the development of new ones. Our evaluation across representative VA tasks demonstrates that VACP-enabled agents achieve higher success rates in interface interpretation and execution compared to current agentic approaches, while reducing token consumption and latency. VACP closes the gap between human-centric VA interfaces and machine perceivability, ensuring agents can reliably act as collaborative users in VA systems.
item.dc:creator: Tobias St\"ahle, P\'eter Ferenc Gyarmati, Thilo Spinner, Rita Sevastjanova, Dominik Moritz, Mennatallah El-Assady

item.title: Vibe Visualizing: How Visualization Novices Try (and Fail) to Generate and Interpret Visualizations with Conversational AI
item.description: arXiv:2606.08914v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conversational AI lowers technical barriers to generating and interpreting visualizations. People without visualization training or practical experience can therefore perform these tasks, but may lack the expertise needed to evaluate the resulting charts and interpretations. Through a study with 20 visualization novices, we examine conversation logs from 60 sessions with ChatGPT and develop a codebook that characterizes participant and AI behaviors in AI-assisted visualization. Paired with interview transcripts and survey responses, we derive three themes under outcome quality, AI non-compliance, and trust, verification, and repair. An exploratory role analysis identifies two session-level roles distinguished by user initiative and associated with different failure patterns. A comparative analysis with Gemini and Claude further reveals distinct system-specific behaviors. Based on these findings, we derive five design recommendations for AI-assisted visualization design and discuss implications for visualization literacy, human-AI roles, accountability, and agentic visualization.
item.dc:creator: Sam Yu-Te Lee, Yun-Hsin Kuo, Chifang Chou, Matthew Ward, Xiwei Xuan, Kwan-Liu Ma

item.title: HANSEL: Interactive Evidence for Post-Hoc Verification of Web Agents
item.description: arXiv:2606.18671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI web agents can perform complex tasks, such as searching for products and making purchases on users' behalf. However, verifying an agent's output remains difficult, because existing transparency mechanisms (e.g., full trajectory logs) require users to review logs and explanations, keeping verification a passive reading task. In this work, we view agent verification as an interactive activity and present HANSEL. Given an agent trajectory, HANSEL extracts evidence pages and snippets and presents them as navigable, live views that preserve relevant page state (e.g., applied filters), allowing users to verify how the agent arrived at its answer through interaction. In a controlled user study with 14 participants, we show that HANSEL significantly reduces task completion time and perceived effort, demonstrating that reframing verification as an interactive activity enables more efficient post-hoc verification of AI agents.
item.dc:creator: Yujin Zhang, Yeonju Hwang, Daye Nam

item.title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
item.description: arXiv:2607.21394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation (CRAFT), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

item.title: IF:CARGO: LLM-Based Semantic Compilation for Al-Native Rule Programming Games
item.description: arXiv:2608.12195v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This case study presents IF: CARGO, an experimental puzzle game that uses a large language model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous game-playing agent. Players author IF/THEN rules in natural language, which the model translates into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine. This architecture creates a playable loop of expression, execution, observation, and revision, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels examined player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role. Results suggest that players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback, while periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands. The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.
item.dc:creator: Ting-Chen Hsu, Lianye Zhang, Jiangxu Lin, Zhaoyi Yu, Fei Qin, Zihao Chen

item.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.39869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.
item.dc:creator: Elena C. Cuffari, Marta P\'erez-Verdugo, Xabier E. Barandiaran

item.title: Measuring the collaboration, not the agent
item.description: arXiv:2611.06487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmarks for visualization agents score the agent alone; the human only supplies reference answers. For high-dimensional data this misses what matters: the knowledge of which variables count is held by on-site experts, not by the model, so the useful question is how well an analyst and an agent do together. We study one specific form of collaboration, the agent proposes a view, the analyst accepts, rejects, or modifies it, and those judgments are kept for later sessions, and propose five measures for it: complementarity, intervention efficiency, appropriate reliance, knowledge retention, and agency. The first four are computed from interaction logs alone. We test the measures, not people: in a testbed for parallel-coordinates design on public manufacturing data (UCI SECOM), with a simulated analyst whose behavior we control, all four are computable and respond to the controlled differences. Whether they reveal anything about real analysts is the next step; we release the testbed for it.
item.dc:creator: Xinxiao Li, Eisei Nakahara

item.title: Understanding Developer Information Needs for Software with Embedded Natural Language Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2507.17264v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Developers use foundation models (FMs) to create novel forms of intelligent software by writing natural language prompts embedded within a software's implementation---referred to as embedded prompts---that are also passed as a string within an FM's API. Developing software with embedded prompts requires developers to engage in iterative embedded prompt changes to obtain the desired behavior. While the information needs of traditional software have been investigated, the information needs of modern developers for embedded prompt changes are underexplored, despite these needs shaping how developers plan and justify embedded prompt changes. In this work, we perform a mixed-method exploratory study on the information needs of developers making changes to embedded prompts. We create, refine, validate, and apply a list of 50 information needs that developers have while making a change to an embedded prompt by interviewing 16 developers, observing 8 developers make prompt changes, surveying 50 developers, and evaluating 72 research and commercial tools. We find that embedded prompts are not well-supported by existing tools: 16 of the 50 information needs, including four of the most important ones, are unaddressed. We conclude with important design opportunities that should be addressed by future developer tools for embedded prompts.
item.dc:creator: Jenny T. Liang, Chenyang Yang, Agnia Sergeyuk, Travis D. Breaux, Brad A. Myers

item.title: NeuroRVQ: Multi-Scale Biosignal Tokenization for Generative Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2510.13068v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Biosignals such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), and electromyography (EMG) encode physiological activity across multiple temporal and spectral scales, yielding representations that are rich but challenging for machine learning. Foundation models trained to predict masked signal tokens have shown promise in learning generalizable biosignal representations, yet their performance depends on the tokenizer's ability to preserve high-frequency dynamics and reconstruct signals with high fidelity. We introduce NeuroRVQ, a modality-adaptive biosignal tokenizer family designed for high-fidelity signal reconstruction. To capture the full frequency spectrum, NeuroRVQ decomposes biosignals into frequency-specific representations via multi-scale temporal convolutions, each encoded into hierarchical RVQ codebooks to preserve high-frequency detail, combined with a novel phase-aware training loss that respects the circular topology of Fourier phase. By tuning the temporal resolution, number and size of temporal kernels and RVQ depth, this design adapts to the spectro-temporal characteristics of each biosignal modality. To validate that tokenizer quality drives downstream performance, we train a simple masked-token foundation model for each modality (NeuroRVQ-FM) using the corresponding NeuroRVQ tokenizer. The NeuroRVQ-FM family achieves competitive or superior downstream performance compared to existing modality-specific foundation models, demonstrating that high-fidelity tokenization is a critical factor for effective biosignal modeling.

item.title: Natural Language Interfaces for Databases: What Changes for SQL-Literate Users?
item.description: arXiv:2511.14718v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural Language Interfaces for Databases (NLIDBs) let users query data in everyday language instead of SQL, and modern systems translate most questions accurately. Does an NLIDB remove the work of querying, or move it? We compared SQL-LLM, a GPT-4o-backed NLIDB, with Snowflake, a manual-SQL platform. Twenty SQL-literate professionals and graduate students, ten per interface, each completed 12 BIRD benchmark tasks with hints naming target columns and operators. SQL-LLM cut completion time per query by 31%. It did not improve accuracy: SQL-LLM users answered 46% of queries correctly versus 64% for Snowflake, a gap this sample cannot confirm ($p = 0.08$) that narrows to 14 points without one session where the system timed out. Think-aloud audio from 11 participants (4 SQL-LLM, 7 Snowflake) showed how the work shifted: SQL-LLM users left initial schema navigation to the model, mainly on easier tasks, and focused on checking the generated SQL, while Snowflake users explored the schema and wrote queries by hand. Coded behavior rates did not differ detectably between arms, and positive remarks during a task did not reliably predict a correct answer. The evidence fits a reallocation of querying work, not its removal: users still had to check the generated SQL.

item.title: The Trajectory Alignment Coefficient in Two Acts: From Reward Tuning to Reward Learning
item.description: arXiv:2601.16906v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The success of RL is fundamentally tied to having a reward function that accurately reflects the task objective. Yet, designing reward functions is time-consuming and prone to misspecification. To address this, our first goal is to understand how to support RL practitioners in specifying reward functions. We leverage the Trajectory Alignment Coefficient (TAC), a metric that evaluates how closely a reward function's induced preferences match those of a domain expert. To test whether TAC provides meaningful support, we evaluated its impact in a user study where practitioners designed reward functions for Lunar Lander. We found that iterative TAC feedback allowed participants to design more performant reward functions while reporting lower cognitive workload than unguided reward design. However, the study also underscored that manual reward design, even with TAC, remains labor-intensive. This motivated our second goal: to learn a reward model that maximizes TAC directly. Specifically, we propose Soft-TAC, a differentiable approximation of TAC that can be used as a loss function to train reward models from human preferences. Our theoretical analysis guarantees that under Soft-TAC optimization: (1) the optimal reward function belongs exclusively to the set of human-aligned reward functions, and (2) this optimal reward remains invariant whether trained on clean or noisy preference data. Empirically, we first evaluate reward models trained with Soft-TAC across three robotic tasks, demonstrating that they consistently match or outperform those trained with the Cross-Entropy loss. Next, we evaluate Soft-TAC in the GT7 driving simulator, and find that Soft-TAC-trained reward models more successfully capture preference-specific driving styles. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that TAC can serve as both a practical tool for guiding reward design and a reward learning objective in complex domains.

item.title: ComplLLM: Fine-tuning LLMs to Discover Complementary Signals for Decision-making
item.description: arXiv:2602.19458v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. We propose ComplLLM, a post-training framework based on decision theory that fine-tunes a decision-assistant LLM to output signals that complement existing agent decisions, using complementary information as reward. We validate ComplLLM on synthetic and real-world tasks involving domain experts, demonstrating how the approach recovers known complementary information, produces plausible explanations of complementary signals to support downstream decision-makers, and improves human and LLM agent decision performance in controlled studies.
item.dc:creator: Ziyang Guo, Yifan Wu, Jason Hartline, Kenneth Holstein, Jessica Hullman

item.title: Do Semantic Distance Tests Actually Predict Creativity in LLMs? Evidence for Jagged Creativity
item.description: arXiv:2605.13450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Measuring the creativity of large language models (LLMs) is essential for designing methods that can improve creativity and for enhancing our scientific understanding of this ability. To accomplish this, it has become common in recent years to administer semantic distance tests of human creativity to LLMs. Although these tests provide a convenient and fully automated way to score aspects of "creativity," their validity as measures of machine creativity has not been established. To address this problem, we conduct the first large-scale, systematic study assessing the effectiveness of semantic distance tests for predicting the creative achievement of LLMs across four target constructs: (a) creative writing, (b) output diversity on open-ended prompts, (c) combinatorial creativity, and (d) scientific ideation. We score each test on two criteria (validity and specificity), and derive a theoretical limit for the maximum attainable specificity and validity a test can achieve. We find that: (1) No test is a significant predictor of output diversity, suggesting that point creativity, the ability to produce a single response connecting semantically distant concepts, and distributional creativity, the ability to produce distinct responses across repeated samples, may dissociate in current LLMs--a pattern we call jagged creativity. (2) The Remote Associates Test is effectively a proxy for general capabilities rather than a specific predictor of creativity in LLMs. (3) Lastly, the Divergent Association Task is the best predictor of creative writing, but no single test predicts all constructs well. In summary, our results prescribe caution when applying psychometric tests and tasks of creativity validated among human populations to LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Schapiro, Alexi Gladstone, Jonah Black, Heng Ji

item.title: Viverra: Text-to-Code with Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2605.14972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A fundamental limitation of Text-to-Code is that no guarantee can be obtained about the correctness of the generated code. Therefore, to ensure its correctness, the generated code still has to be reviewed, tested, and maintained by developers. However, parsing through LLM-generated code can be tedious and time-consuming, potentially negating the productivity gains promised by AI-coding tools. To address this challenge, we present Viverra, a system that automatically produces formally verified annotations alongside generated code to aid user's understanding of the generated program. Given a natural-language task description, Viverra prompts an LLM to synthesize a C program together with candidate assertions expressing safety and correctness properties. It then verifies those assertions in a compositional and best-effort manner via a portfolio of bounded model checkers. Evaluation on 17 diverse programming tasks suggests that Viverra can efficiently generate code with verified assertions, and that these assertions improve users' performance on code-comprehension tasks in a user study with more than 400 task completions.
item.dc:creator: Haoze Wu, Rocky Klopfenstein, Keith Farkas, Nina Narodytska
